prompt.en: Make the computer say hello. Use print to show the words Hello, world! on the screen.

starter: # Write your code here.

en: Use the print function to show something on the screen.
Text goes inside quote marks, inside the brackets: print("...").
Type the words exactly: capital H, a comma, and an exclamation mark at the end.

explain.en: print(...) shows what is inside the brackets. Words must be inside quote marks, like "hi".

guided.solution: print("hi")

solution: print("Hello, world!")

solution_note.en: print shows text. The words are inside quote marks so Python knows they are text.

prompt.en: Write a function called double. It takes a number n and gives back n times 2.

en: A function gives a value back with the word return.
The body of your function is one line: return, then n times 2.

explain.en: return sends a value out of the function. For now, just give back n itself.

guided.solution:
def double(n):
    return n

explain.en: Change what you return. In Python, * means times.

guided.solution:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

solution:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

solution_note.en: return n * 2 hands back the answer to whoever called the function.

prompt.en: Write a function count_evens(numbers). It gets a list of whole numbers and gives back how many of them are even.

en: An even number has no remainder when you divide it by 2.
The % sign gives the remainder. 7 % 2 is 1, and 8 % 2 is 0.
Keep a counter. Loop over the list. If n % 2 == 0, add 1 to the counter. Return the counter.

goal.en: Make a counter and give it back.

explain.en: A counter is a variable that starts at 0. Return it at the end.

goal.en: Loop over the list and count every number.

explain.en: for n in numbers: runs the lines below it once for each number. Add 1 to count each time.

name.en: It counts every item (all of these are even)

explain.en: Put the counting line inside an if. The test n % 2 == 0 is true for even numbers.

solution_note.en: n % 2 == 0 is true when n divides by 2 with nothing left over. The counter goes up only then.

prompt.en: Write a function reverse_words(sentence). It gives back the same words in the opposite order, joined by single spaces. Example: "one two three" becomes "three two one". Extra spaces at the ends or in the middle are ignored.

name.en: An empty sentence gives an empty string

en: Start by splitting the sentence into a list of words with .split().
A list can be turned around with words[::-1].
Put the words back together with " ".join(your_list).

explain.en: .split() turns "a b" into the list ["a", "b"]. It also ignores extra spaces.

name.en: It gives a list of words

explain.en: words[::-1] gives the list in reverse order.

solution_note.en: split makes a list, [::-1] reverses it, and join glues the words back into one string.

prompt.en: Write a function fizzbuzz(n). It gives back a list for the numbers 1 to n. For each number, put in the text "Fizz" if it divides by 3, "Buzz" if it divides by 5, and "FizzBuzz" if it divides by both. Otherwise put the number as text, like "7".

en: range(1, n + 1) gives the numbers from 1 up to n.
i % 3 == 0 means i divides by 3 with nothing left over.
Check for both 3 and 5 first (divides by 15). If you check 3 first, you never reach FizzBuzz.

goal.en: Make a list of the numbers as text.

explain.en: str(5) turns the number 5 into the text "5". result.append(x) adds x to the end of a list.
Inside the loop, use if i % 3 == 0: to add "Fizz" instead of the number.

solution_note.en: A number that divides by both 3 and 5 divides by 15, so that check comes first.

prompt.en: Write a function to_binary(n). It gives back the binary digits of a whole number n (0 or more) as text. Example: 5 becomes "101". Do not use the built-in bin() function.

preamble:
def bin(*args, **kwargs):
    raise NameError('Please do not use bin().')

en: The last binary digit of n is n % 2. Then divide n by 2 with // and repeat until n is 0.
The digits come out last-first. Put each new digit at the front of the text, not the end.
Zero is a special case: its answer is "0", but the loop would give an empty text.

explain.en: A number's last binary digit is its remainder when you divide by 2. n % 2 is 0 or 1. Give it back as text.

guided.solution:
def to_binary(n):
    return str(n % 2)

goal.en: Collect every digit, even if they come out backwards.

explain.en: Repeat while n > 0: add the last digit, then do n = n // 2 to drop it. The digits will be in reverse order for now.

solution_note.en: Each step peels off the last binary digit. Putting new digits at the front fixes the order.

prompt.en: Make the computer say hello. Use console.log to show the words Hello, world! on the screen.

starter: // Write your code here.

en: Use console.log to show something on the screen.
Text goes inside quote marks, inside the brackets: console.log("...");
Type the words exactly: capital H, a comma, and an exclamation mark at the end.

explain.en: console.log(...) shows what is inside the brackets. Words must be inside quote marks, like "hi".

guided.solution: console.log("hi");

solution: console.log("Hello, world!");

solution_note.en: console.log shows text. The words are inside quote marks so JavaScript knows they are text.

prompt.en: Write a function called add. It takes two numbers, a and b, and gives back their sum.

en: A function gives a value back with the word return.
In JavaScript, the + sign adds two numbers.
The body is one line: return, then a plus b, then a semicolon.

explain.en: return sends a value out of the function. For now, just give back a.

solution_note.en: return a + b; hands the sum back to whoever called the function.

prompt.en: Write a function findMax(numbers). It gives back the biggest number in the list. If the list is empty, give back null. Do not use Math.max.

name.en: One number is its own biggest

en: Keep a variable for the biggest number you have seen so far.
Start it as the first item. Then look at the other items one by one.
If an item is bigger than your variable, put that item in the variable. Handle the empty list first.

explain.en: numbers.length is how many items there are. If it is 0, return null.

goal.en: Start with the first number as the biggest.

explain.en: numbers[0] is the first item. Keep it in a variable called biggest and return that.

name.en: One number is its own biggest

explain.en: Use for (const n of numbers) { ... }. If n is bigger than biggest, set biggest = n.

solution_note.en: The variable biggest always holds the largest number seen so far.

prompt.en: Write a function countVowels(text). It gives back how many vowels (a, e, i, o, u) are in the text. Capital letters count too.

en: You can loop over the letters of a text with for (const ch of text).
"aeiou".includes(ch) is true when ch is a vowel.
Capital letters are not in "aeiou". Make the text lower case first with text.toLowerCase().

explain.en: for (const ch of text) goes through the text one letter at a time. Add 1 to count each time.

name.en: It counts every letter for now

explain.en: Add an if: "aeiou".includes(ch) is true when ch is a vowel. Only then add 1.

solution_note.en: toLowerCase makes A and a the same, so one check finds both.

prompt.en: Write a function sortNumbers(numbers). It gives back a NEW list with the same numbers from smallest to biggest. Do not change the list you were given, and do not use .sort().

name.en: The original list is not changed

en: Make a copy first: const result = [...numbers]; Then change only the copy.
Compare each item with the one next to it. If they are the wrong way round, swap them.
One pass along the list is not enough for every list. Repeat the passes (a loop inside a loop).

goal.en: Make a copy and return it.

explain.en: [...numbers] makes a new list with the same items. Changing the copy leaves the original alone.

tests.code: const a = [2, 1]; const r = sortNumbers(a); assert(Array.isArray(r) && r !== a, "Return a new list, not the same one.")

goal.en: Make one pass: swap neighbours that are the wrong way round.

explain.en: Loop i from 0 to length - 2. If result[i] > result[i + 1], swap them using a temporary variable.

solution_note.en: Each pass pushes the biggest remaining number to the end. This is called bubble sort.

prompt.en: Write a function binarySearch(sorted, target). The list is sorted from smallest to biggest. Give back the position (index) of target, or -1 if it is not there. Do it by halving the part you search each time.

tests.code: const big = Array.from({ length: 1000 }, (_, i) => i * 2); assertEqual(binarySearch(big, 998), 499); assertEqual(binarySearch(big, 999), -1)

en: Keep two positions, low and high. The target can only be between them.
Look at the middle item: mid = Math.floor((low + high) / 2). Is it the target, too small, or too big?
If the middle is too small, the target is on the right: set low = mid + 1. If too big, set high = mid - 1. Stop when low is more than high.

explain.en: Math.floor(sorted.length / 2) is the middle position. If that item is the target, return its position. Otherwise return -1 for now.

goal.en: Search the right half when the middle is too small.

explain.en: Use low and high and a while (low <= high) loop. When sorted[mid] < target, set low = mid + 1. For now, if the middle is too big, just return -1.

solution_note.en: Each step throws away half of the list, so 1000 items need only about 10 looks.

prompt.en: Write a function greet(name). It gives back the text Hello, then a space, then the name, then an exclamation mark. Example: greet("Sam") gives "Hello, Sam!".

en: Text can be joined with the + sign: "ab" + "cd" is "abcd".
You need three pieces: "Hello, ", the name, and "!".
Join the three pieces with + and return the result. Watch the space after the comma.

explain.en: Text goes inside quote marks. return sends it back.

guided.solution:
def greet(name):
    return "Hello"

explain.en: Use + to join two pieces of text: "Hello, " + name.

guided.solution:
def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name

solution:
def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name + "!"

solution_note.en: + joins pieces of text together, in the order you write them.

prompt.en: Write a function is_even(n). It gives back True if the whole number n is even, and False if it is odd.

name.en: It gives True or False, not a number

tests.code: assert type(is_even(4)) is bool, "Give back True or False."

en: An even number divides by 2 with nothing left over.
n % 2 is the remainder when n is divided by 2.
Compare that remainder with 0 using ==. The answer of a comparison is already True or False.

explain.en: n % 2 gives the remainder of n divided by 2. It is 0 for even numbers and 1 for odd numbers.

guided.solution:
def is_even(n):
    return n % 2

solution:
def is_even(n):
    return n % 2 == 0

solution_note.en: n % 2 == 0 asks: is the remainder zero? The answer is True or False.

prompt.en: Write a function is_palindrome(text). It gives back True if the text reads the same forwards and backwards, and False if not. Ignore capital letters and spaces. Example: "Race car" is a palindrome.

name.en: Capital letters and spaces are ignored

tests.code: check(is_palindrome("A man a plan a canal Panama"), True)
assert type(is_palindrome("a")) is bool, "Give back True or False."

en: First make the text easy to compare: all lower case, and no spaces.
Text can be reversed with text[::-1]. A palindrome is equal to its own reverse.

explain.en: text.lower() makes every letter small. .replace(" ", "") takes the spaces out.
cleaned[::-1] is the same text backwards.

solution_note.en: A palindrome is the same as its own reverse, so we compare the cleaned text with it.

prompt.en: Write a function word_count(text). It gives back a dictionary that says how many times each word appears. Ignore capital letters: Go and go are the same word. Words are separated by spaces. Example: word_count("the cat the") gives {"the": 2, "cat": 1}.

name.en: Empty text gives an empty dictionary

en: Make the text lower case, then split it into a list of words.
A dictionary links a word to a number: counts["cat"] = 1. Start with an empty one: {}.
For each word, add 1 to its count. counts.get(word, 0) gives 0 if the word is new.

goal.en: Make a list of lower-case words.

explain.en: text.lower().split() gives the words in small letters, as a list.

guided.solution:
def word_count(text):
    return text.lower().split()

goal.en: Put every word in a dictionary.

explain.en: Start with counts = {}. For each word, set counts[word] = 1 for now.

solution_note.en: counts.get(word, 0) is the old count, or 0 for a new word. Adding 1 gives the new count.

prompt.en: Computers can spot mistakes by adding one extra digit. Write a function add_parity_bit(bits). The text bits is made of 0s and 1s. Add one more digit at the end (0 or 1) so that the whole text has an EVEN number of 1s. Example: "101" becomes "1010", and "111" becomes "1111".

en: Count the 1s in the text with bits.count("1").
If the count is odd, add a 1 to make it even. If it is already even, add a 0.
count % 2 is 1 when the count is odd and 0 when it is even. Turn it into text with str() and put it on the end.

explain.en: bits.count("1") tells you how many 1s are in the text.
ones % 2 is 1 for an odd count and 0 for an even count. That is the digit you need to add.

solution:
def add_parity_bit(bits):
    return bits + str(bits.count("1") % 2)

solution_note.en: The extra digit makes the number of 1s even. If one digit gets flipped later, the count turns odd and the mistake shows.

prompt.en: Write a function primes_up_to(n). It gives back a list of every prime number from 2 up to n (n included), smallest first. A prime has no divisors except 1 and itself. Example: primes_up_to(10) gives [2, 3, 5, 7].

name.en: There are no primes up to 1

en: Look at each number i from 2 to n. Decide if i is prime, and keep it if it is.
To test i, try dividing by d = 2, 3, 4 ... If i % d == 0 for any d, then i is not prime.
You only need to try d while d * d <= i. That makes it much faster.

goal.en: List the numbers from 2 to n.

explain.en: range(2, n + 1) counts from 2 up to n. list(...) turns it into a list.

guided.solution:
def primes_up_to(n):
    return list(range(2, n + 1))

explain.en: Keep a number if it is 2, or if i % 2 != 0. A list can be built with a loop and append.

name.en: Evens are gone (9 is still there for now)

solution_note.en: If i has a divisor, it has one that is at most the square root of i. So we can stop trying at d * d > i.

prompt.en: Write a function flatten(items). The list items can hold numbers and also other lists, and those lists can hold lists too, as deep as you like. Give back one flat list with all the numbers in the same order. Example: flatten([1, [2, [3]], 4]) gives [1, 2, 3, 4].

en: Go through the items one by one and build a new list called result.
isinstance(item, list) is True when item is itself a list.
If item is a list, flatten it too (your function can call itself!) and add everything it gives back. Otherwise add item.

goal.en: Copy the items into a new list.

explain.en: result = [] makes an empty list. result.append(x) adds x to the end.

name.en: A flat list stays the same

goal.en: Open up the lists inside, one level deep.

explain.en: If item is a list, loop over it and append each inner item. Otherwise append item.

solution_note.en: A list inside a list is flattened by the same function. That is called recursion.

prompt.en: Write a function greet(name). It gives back the text Hello, then a space, then the name, then an exclamation mark. Example: greet("Sam") gives "Hello, Sam!".

en: Text can be joined with the + sign: "ab" + "cd" is "abcd".
You need three pieces: "Hello, ", the name, and "!".
Join the three pieces with + and return the result. Watch the space after the comma.

explain.en: Text goes inside quote marks. return sends it back.

tests.code: assert(greet("x").startsWith("Hello"), "The greeting should start with Hello.")

explain.en: Use + to join two pieces of text: "Hello, " + name.

solution_note.en: + joins pieces of text together, in the order you write them.

prompt.en: Write a function sum(numbers). It gives back the total of all the numbers in the list. An empty list gives 0.

en: Keep a variable called total that starts at 0.
for (const n of numbers) { ... } goes through the numbers one at a time.
Inside the loop, add n to total. After the loop, return total.

explain.en: let total = 0; makes a variable. Return it. An empty list should give 0.

goal.en: Add each number to the total.

explain.en: total += n means total = total + n.

solution_note.en: total collects the numbers one at a time, so after the loop it holds the whole sum.

prompt.en: Write a function reverseString(text). It gives back the same text backwards. Example: "abc" becomes "cba". Do not use .reverse().

en: Build a new text one letter at a time. Start with an empty text: "".
for (const ch of text) goes through the letters from first to last.
If you put each new letter at the FRONT of your result (ch + result), the order flips.

goal.en: Copy the letters one by one.

explain.en: Start with let result = ""; Add each letter to the end with result += ch.

solution_note.en: Each new letter goes in front of the ones before it, so the last letter ends up first.

prompt.en: The factorial of n (written n!) is 1 x 2 x 3 x ... x n. For example 5! = 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 120. Write a function factorial(n) that gives it back. 0! is 1.

en: 5! means 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1. And 0! is 1.
Start a variable called result at 1. Then multiply it by each whole number from 1 up to n.
Use a loop: for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++). Multiply result by i inside it.

explain.en: result = 1 is the starting point. It is also the right answer for 0!.

goal.en: Multiply by every number up to n.

explain.en: for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) runs once for each i. Do result *= i inside.

solution_note.en: For 0 the loop does not run, so the answer stays 1, which is right.

prompt.en: The Fibonacci numbers go 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 ... Each one is the sum of the two before it. Write a function fibonacci(n) that gives back the n-th one, counting from 0: fibonacci(0) is 0, fibonacci(1) is 1, fibonacci(7) is 13. It must also work fast for n = 50.

en: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 ...
If your function calls itself twice, it repeats a huge amount of work for n = 50. Use a loop instead.
Keep two variables, previous and current. In each step make next = previous + current, then move previous and current forward.

explain.en: For n = 0 the answer is 0, and for n = 1 it is 1. So if n < 2, return n.

goal.en: Walk along the sequence with a loop.

explain.en: Start with previous = 0 and current = 1. Repeat n - 1 times: next = previous + current, then previous = current and current = next.

solution_note.en: The loop only ever remembers the last two numbers, so it takes n steps. Calling the function twice from itself would take billions.
